title: Cost-Based Model Selection via ROC
reviewer_facing_definition:
Cost-based model selection via ROC means choosing among candidate ROC operating points by comparing their expected costs rather than selecting a model from TPR or FPR alone.

Each candidate is represented by an ROC point (FPR, TPR). Its expected cost is calculated using the class prior, its TPR and FPR, and the costs associated with false negatives, false positives, true positives, and true negatives.

C(M) = p(1 - TPR)c_FN
     + (1 - p)FPR c_FP
     + p TPR c_TP
     + (1 - p)(1 - FPR)c_TN

The preferred model is the candidate with the lowest expected cost under the given class distribution and cost matrix.

title: Curse of Dimensionality
reviewer_facing_definition:
The curse of dimensionality is the phenomenon that many types of data analysis become significantly harder as the number of dimensions or attributes increases.

As dimensionality increases, the available data become increasingly sparse in the space they occupy. This can make the observed data less representative of the possible data space.

For classification, there may not be enough data to build a model that reliably handles all possible objects. For clustering, differences in density and distances between points become less meaningful, which can lead to poorer-quality clusters.

title: Deletion Strategy
reviewer_facing_definition:
Deletion strategy is a way of handling missing data by removing incomplete data rather than estimating the missing values.

In case deletion, also called ignore missing, every instance that contains at least one missing value is removed from the data set. A related approach is to remove an attribute when it contains a large amount of missing data.

If many cases are deleted, the sample size and statistical power can be substantially reduced, and if the missing data are not missing completely at random, deletion can introduce bias.

title: Intra-cluster Distance
reviewer_facing_definition:
Intra-cluster distance refers to the distance between data points that belong to the same cluster. It is used to describe how close or cohesive the members of a cluster are. In general, smaller intra-cluster distances indicate that the points within the cluster are more closely grouped together.

For an individual point, one intra-cluster distance measure is the average distance from that point to all other points in its own cluster:

a(x) = [sum of d(x,u) for all u in X except x] / (|X| - 1)

where X is the cluster containing x.

title: K-Means Algorithm
reviewer_facing_definition:
K-Means is a partitional clustering algorithm that divides a data set into a user-specified number K of clusters, with each cluster represented by a centroid.

The basic algorithm is:

1. Choose K initial centroids.
2. Assign each data point to its closest centroid.
3. Recompute the centroid of each cluster from the points assigned to it.
4. Repeat the assignment and centroid-update steps until no points change clusters, or equivalently, until the centroids no longer change.

For standard Euclidean K-Means, the centroid of a cluster is the mean of its points, and the objective is to minimize the total sum of squared errors (SSE), which measures the squared distances of points from their assigned centroids.

title: Laplace Estimator
reviewer_facing_definition:
The Laplace estimator is a method for estimating categorical conditional probabilities that prevents unseen attribute-class combinations from receiving probability zero.

Formula:
P(X_i = c | y) = (n_c + 1) / (n + v)

where:
n_c = number of training instances in class y with X_i = c
n = total number of training instances belonging to class y
v = number of possible values of attribute X_i

Its purpose is to avoid the zero-frequency problem, where one zero conditional probability can make the entire class-conditional product zero.

title: Non-Deterministic Search
reviewer_facing_definition:

title: Properties of a Distance Function
reviewer_facing_definition:
A distance function d(x, y) that is a metric satisfies the following properties:

1. Positivity:
   d(x, y) >= 0 for all x and y, and d(x, y) = 0 only if x = y.

2. Symmetry:
   d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x and y.

3. Triangle inequality:
   d(x, z) <= d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all x, y, and z.

A distance measure that satisfies all of these properties is called a metric.

title: SSE Optimization Criterion
reviewer_facing_definition:

title: Bayes' Theorem
reviewer_facing_definition:
Bayes' theorem is a probability rule for updating the probability of a hypothesis after observing evidence.

It is given by

P(H | E) = P(E | H)P(H) / P(E),

where P(H | E) is the posterior probability of the hypothesis after observing the evidence, P(E | H) is the likelihood of observing the evidence if the hypothesis is true, P(H) is the prior probability of the hypothesis before observing the evidence, and P(E) is the overall probability of the evidence.

In classification, the theorem can be written as

P(y | x) = P(x | y)P(y) / P(x).

Naive Bayes makes this practical in high-dimensional classification by factorizing P(x | y) into class-conditional probabilities under the assumption that the attributes are conditionally independent given the class.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor distinguishes Bidirectional Generation from Random Generation: BG combines greedy forward and backward search, whereas RG generates feature subsets using a random search direction.

Bidirectional search is one of three dimensions (along with Search strategy and Evaluation Measure) used to categorize feature selection combinations.

title: Binary Decision Tree
reviewer_facing_definition:
A binary decision tree is a decision tree in which every attribute test used to split a node has exactly two possible outcomes, producing two child nodes.

Binary splits can be applied to different types of attributes. For example, the values of a nominal attribute can be partitioned into two groups, while a continuous attribute can be divided using a threshold condition such as A < v and A ≥ v.

A one-level binary decision tree containing a single split is called a decision stump.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What is a decision stump?
How do you choose the split point in a binary tree?
Why use a validation set for decision trees?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with 'Bushy Decision Tree (Multi-split)' which allows more than two children per node.
do_not_confuse_with: General decision tree induction without the binary constraint

acceptable_teaching_moves: Using a simple one-dimensional attribute example to illustrate a split point.
Comparing two trees using validation error rates to demonstrate model selection.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing a decision stump with a fully grown decision tree.
Assuming a single decision stump provides high accuracy without boosting.
red_flags: Claiming that a decision stump alone is sufficient for complex classification tasks without mentioning ensemble methods like AdaBoost.
what_tutor_should_explain: The relationship between a decision stump and a full binary decision tree.
How the split point k is determined using entropy.
The role of validation error rates in preferring one tree over another.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor clarifies that “binary” in a binary decision tree refers to each split producing two child branches, not necessarily to the classification problem having only two class labels.

evidence_spans.claim: A one-level binary decision tree is also known as a decision stump and uses a test condition (x ≤ k) where k is a split point chosen to minimize leaf node entropy.
Without boosting, the accuracy of a decision stump is limited (e.g., at best 70%).
Validation sets can be used in decision tree induction to calculate error rates and prefer the tree with the lower rate.

title: Bushy Decision Tree (Multi-split)
reviewer_facing_definition:
A multiway split in a decision tree is an attribute test condition that produces more than two outcomes, creating a separate child node for each outcome or partition.

For a nominal attribute, a multiway split can create one outcome for each distinct attribute value. For example, an attribute with three distinct values can produce a three-way split.

Ordinal attributes can also produce multiway splits as long as the grouping preserves their ordering. For continuous attributes, a multiway split can be constructed using mutually exclusive value ranges that together cover the relevant range of the attribute.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What is a bushy decision tree?
How do multi-split trees handle instances covered by multiple rules?
Difference between binary and bushy trees
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Binary Decision Trees, which only allow two-way splits at each node.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Explain the relationship between the tree structure and the resulting rule set ordering.
common_confusions_or_errors: Assuming that a single instance can only be covered by one rule in a multi-split context.
red_flags: Claiming that multi-split trees eliminate the need for rule ordering strategies.
what_tutor_should_explain: How multi-way splits differ from binary splits.
The impact of rule ordering when an instance is covered by multiple rules.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor clarifies that a multiway split gives a decision-tree node more than two possible branches, but a test instance follows the single branch corresponding to its test outcome rather than simultaneously following multiple branches or receiving predictions from multiple tree rules.

evidence_spans.claim: In a rule set, a test instance may be covered by multiple rules, which can assign different class labels based on their position in the set.

title: Chi-Squared Test
reviewer_facing_definition:
The Chi-Squared Test is a statistical test used for categorical variables to determine whether two categorical attributes are independent.

The null hypothesis states that the two attributes are independent. The test compares the observed counts in a contingency table with the counts expected under independence:

χ² = Σi Σj (oij - eij)² / eij,

where oij is the observed count and eij is the expected count.

A larger χ² value indicates a greater departure from independence. If the χ² value exceeds the critical value for the chosen significance level, the null hypothesis of independence is rejected.

In feature selection, dependence between two input features can indicate possible redundancy.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: How do I use the chi-squared test for feature selection?
What is the role of the chi-squared test in selecting variables?
Can we use chi-squared to find interdependent variables?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with other goodness criteria like Information Gain or Pearson Correlation which may measure different types of relationships (e.g., linear vs. independence).

acceptable_teaching_moves: Asking the student to identify which variables are being tested for interdependence.
Explaining the relationship between significance levels and variable selection.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing the chi-squared test with measures of joint information like normalized surprisal.
red_flags: Applying the test without defining a significance level.
what_tutor_should_explain: The purpose of the test in selecting interdependent variables.
The concept of a 'presumed significant level' in the context of the test.

evidence_spans.claim: A chi-squared test is used to select interdependent variables in X at a presumed significant level.

title: Classification Threshold (Cutoff)
reviewer_facing_definition:
A classification threshold, or cutoff, is a value applied to a classifier's score to convert the score into a predicted class label.

In binary classification, an instance is predicted as positive when its positive-class score exceeds the chosen threshold, and as negative otherwise.

Changing the threshold changes the resulting classification outcomes and therefore affects measures such as true positive rate, false positive rate, precision, and recall. The threshold can be selected according to the desired evaluation criterion or decision objective.
sibling_kc_names: Threshold Effect on Precision, Recall, F1

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: How do we choose a threshold for accuracy?
What happens if a good classifier falls below the accuracy cutoff?
Selecting a suitable threshold for the classifier
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with ROC Curve or AUC, which evaluate performance across all possible thresholds rather than a single fixed accuracy cutoff.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Ask the student to consider the impact of natural variability on a classifier's observed accuracy relative to a fixed cutoff.
common_confusions_or_errors: Assuming a classifier is 'bad' simply because it falls below a specific accuracy threshold without considering data variability.
red_flags: Ignoring the possibility of false rejections when applying a strict accuracy threshold.
what_tutor_should_explain: The relationship between the chosen accuracy threshold and the probability of falsely rejecting a valid classifier.
How natural variability in data can cause a good classifier to perform below a fixed threshold.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor distinguishes a classification score threshold, which converts model scores into class predictions, from a threshold placed on an evaluation measure such as accuracy to decide whether a classifier is considered effective.

evidence_spans.claim: A threshold for classification accuracy can be used to identify effective classifiers.
Choosing a threshold for accuracy carries the risk of falsely rejecting a good classifier if its accuracy is lower than the threshold due to natural variability in the data.

title: Comparing Two Models on Independent Test Sets
canonical_name: Comparing Two Models on Independent Test Sets
reviewer_facing_definition:
When two classification models are evaluated on two independent test sets, their observed error rates can be compared to determine whether the difference in performance is statistically significant.

If model M1 has error rate e1 on a test set of size n1 and model M2 has error rate e2 on an independent test set of size n2, the observed difference is

d = e1 - e2.

For sufficiently large test sets, the error rates can be approximated by normal distributions, and the variance of the difference can be estimated as

σd² ≈ e1(1 - e1)/n1 + e2(1 - e2)/n2.

A confidence interval for the true difference in error rates can then be used to judge statistical significance. If the confidence interval includes 0, the observed difference is not statistically significant at that confidence level.
source_hierarchy_path: Comparing Two Models on Independent Test Sets

matching_cues: predict class labels of instances it has never encountered
likely_dialogue_surface_forms: How do I know which of these two models is better?
Why do we need a separate test set for model comparison?
Can I use the same data for training and testing when comparing models?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with specific statistical tests like McNemar or Friedman tests which may be used for the actual comparison of performance metrics.
do_not_confuse_with: Internal validation/cross-validation on the training set
Single model evaluation without a comparison baseline

acceptable_teaching_moves: Asking the student why a model might perform well on training data but poorly on new data.
Explaining the role of independent test sets in simulating real-world performance.
common_confusions_or_errors: Using the training set to evaluate the model's predictive accuracy (overfitting).
red_flags: Student suggesting that the test set can be a subset of the training set.
what_tutor_should_explain: The definition of generalization performance.
The reason why training and test sets must be independent to avoid biased results.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor distinguishes independence between the two test sets used to compare two models from the separate requirement that training and test data must not overlap.

evidence_spans.claim: Comparing two models can involve comparing two sets of clusters to determine which is superior.
Training and test sets must be independent to ensure the induced model can accurately predict class labels of previously unseen instances.
Models capable of accurately predicting labels for unseen instances are said to have good generalization performance.

title: Conditional Probability (Likelihood)
reviewer_facing_definition: In the context of Naive Bayes, the likelihood refers to the probability of the observed data given a class. Naive Bayes transforms Bayes' theorem into a practical classification tool by factorizing this likelihood into simpler, class-conditional terms, allowing for more efficient computation of the posterior probability.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: How do we handle the likelihood in Naive Bayes?
What does it mean to factorize the likelihood?
Why do we use class-conditional terms?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Prior Probability, which is the probability of the class regardless of the data.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Explain the transition from the general Bayes' theorem to the Naive Bayes practical implementation via factorization.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing the likelihood (P(Data|Class)) with the posterior probability (P(Class|Data)).
red_flags: Failure to distinguish between the joint likelihood and the factorized class-conditional probabilities.
what_tutor_should_explain: How the likelihood is broken down into simpler class-conditional terms to make the classifier practical.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor distinguishes the likelihood P(x | y), which is the probability of observing the data given the class, from the posterior P(y | x), which is the probability of the class after observing the data.

evidence_spans.claim: Naive Bayes makes Bayes' theorem a practical classifier by factorizing the likelihood into simpler class-conditional terms.

title: Cosine Similarity
reviewer_facing_definition:
Cosine similarity measures the similarity between two vectors based on the angle between them, or equivalently, how closely they point in the same direction.

It is calculated as

cos(x, y) = (x · y) / (||x|| ||y||),

where x · y is the dot product of the two vectors and ||x|| and ||y|| are their magnitudes.

A larger cosine similarity indicates greater similarity in direction. For general vectors, cosine similarity ranges from -1 to 1, while for non-negative vectors such as word-count vectors it ranges from 0 to 1.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What is cosine similarity?
How does cosine similarity differ from Euclidean distance?
Is a higher cosine similarity score better?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Manhattan and Euclidean distance, which are distance measures where smaller values indicate closer proximity.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Comparing cosine similarity directly against Euclidean or Manhattan distance to highlight the inverse relationship between distance and similarity.
common_confusions_or_errors: Assuming that a smaller score means the objects are more similar (confusing similarity with distance).
red_flags: Tutor stating that a low cosine similarity score indicates high similarity.
what_tutor_should_explain: The fundamental difference between a distance measure and a similarity score.
The relationship between the magnitude of the score and the degree of similarity.

evidence_spans.claim: Cosine similarity is a similarity score where a larger value indicates greater similarity.
Cosine similarity differs from Manhattan and Euclidean distance, as the latter are distance measures where smaller values mean closer proximity.

title: Cost Matrix
reviewer_facing_definition:
A cost matrix specifies the cost associated with each possible classification outcome.

For binary classification, it can assign separate costs to true negatives, false positives, false negatives, and true positives. These costs are used in cost-sensitive evaluation to calculate the expected cost of a classifier.

The preferred classifier is the one that minimizes the expected cost under the given cost matrix.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What is a cost matrix?
How do we use a cost matrix for imbalanced data?
minimizes expected cost under the given cost matrix
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Cost-Sensitive Classification, which is the broader approach of incorporating these costs into the learning process.
do_not_confuse_with: Confusion matrix (which counts errors but does not necessarily assign weights/costs to them)

acceptable_teaching_moves: Asking the student to define the cost of a false negative in a specific domain (e.g., medical diagnosis).
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing the cost matrix with a standard confusion matrix.
red_flags: Student treats all classification errors as having equal cost.
what_tutor_should_explain: The purpose of assigning different weights to false positives versus false negatives.
How the cost matrix influences the decision boundary of a classifier.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor clarifies that a cost matrix can assign costs or rewards to correct outcomes as well as to classification errors, and that “cost” need not represent monetary cost.

evidence_spans.claim: The properties of a cost matrix have been studied by Elkan.

title: Cost-Sensitive Classification
reviewer_facing_definition: Cost-sensitive classification is an approach used when the cost of misclassifying a class with lower probability is significantly higher than other misclassification costs. While probabilistic classifiers typically assign an instance to the class with the highest probability score, cost-sensitive classification adjusts this decision process to account for these disparate costs. This topic is specifically relevant when dealing with probabilistic outputs from classifiers.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What happens if misclassifying the minority class is more expensive?
How does cost-sensitive classification work with probabilistic classifiers?
Why wouldn't we just pick the class with the highest probability?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with standard probabilistic classification where the highest probability always determines the class label regardless of cost.
do_not_confuse_with: Simple probability thresholding without cost considerations

acceptable_teaching_moves: Asking the student to consider a scenario where a False Negative is much more costly than a False Positive (e.g., medical diagnosis).
common_confusions_or_errors: Assuming that the class with the highest probability is always the optimal choice in a real-world scenario with asymmetric costs.
red_flags: Confusing cost-sensitive classification with simple oversampling or undersampling techniques.
what_tutor_should_explain: The difference between assigning a label based on the highest probability versus assigning it based on the cost of error.
The role of probabilistic classifiers in providing the confidence scores necessary for cost-sensitive decisions.

evidence_spans.claim: Cost-sensitive classification is applied when the cost of misclassifying the class with lower probability is significantly higher than the alternative.
Cost-sensitive classification is discussed in the context of classifiers with probabilistic outputs.

title: Covariance
reviewer_facing_definition: Covariance is a widely used statistical measure employed to determine the extent to which two variables change together. In the context of data processing and imputation, it can be represented as a covariance matrix, which may be separated into observed and missing values. Additionally, the concept extends to the conditional covariance matrix, specifically used to describe the imputation error.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What is covariance?
How do we use the covariance matrix in imputation?
What does it mean for variables to change together?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Pearson Product-Moment Correlation or Spearman Rank Correlation, which are also goodness criteria for feature selection.
do_not_confuse_with: Correlation coefficient (though similar, they are distinct measures)

acceptable_teaching_moves: Comparing covariance to correlation to highlight their shared purpose of measuring variable relationships.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing covariance with correlation.
red_flags: Providing a correlation coefficient range (-1 to 1) as the range for covariance.
what_tutor_should_explain: The basic definition of covariance as a measure of how two variables change together.
The role of the covariance matrix in handling missing data and imputation errors.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor clarifies that zero covariance does not in general imply that two variables are independent.

evidence_spans.claim: Covariance is a statistical measure used to check how much two variables change together.
Covariance can be represented as a covariance matrix, which can be separated into observed and missing values.
The conditional covariance matrix is used to represent the imputation error.

title: Density-Connected
reviewer_facing_definition:
In DBSCAN, two points p and q are density-connected if there exists a point o such that both p and q are density-reachable from o.

Density-connected points therefore do not need to be directly within ε of each other. Their connection can be established through chains of density-reachable points originating from a common point.

How does SUBCLU use density-connectivity?
Is this related to DBSCAN density connectivity?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with 'Density-Reachable' or 'Directly Density-Reachable' as these are related DBSCAN concepts.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Linking the concept to the broader DBSCAN framework.
Introducing SUBCLU as an application of density-connected subspace clustering.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing density-connectivity with simple reachability.
red_flags: Providing a definition of density-connectivity that is not grounded in the provided evidence.
what_tutor_should_explain: The relationship between density-connectivity and the DBSCAN algorithm.
How SUBCLU extends these concepts to subspace clustering.

evidence_spans.claim: SUBCLU (density-connected SUBspace CLUstering) is a subspace clustering algorithm based on DBSCAN.

title: Density-Reachable
reviewer_facing_definition:
In DBSCAN, a point q is density-reachable from a point p if there exists a sequence of points

p = p1, p2, ..., pn = q

such that each point pi+1 is directly density-reachable from the preceding point pi.

Density-reachability therefore extends direct density-reachability through a chain of dense neighborhoods, allowing two points to be related even when they are not directly within ε of each other.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What does it mean for a point to be density-reachable?
Is this point density-reachable from the core point?
How do we determine if a point is reachable?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with 'Directly Density-Reachable' and 'Density-Connected'.
Distinguish between the properties of a core point versus a border point.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Asking the student to identify if a point is a core point before determining if other points are reachable from it.
Using a visual example to show a point that is not core but is within epsilon of one.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing a border point with a core point.
Assuming any point within epsilon of another point is automatically density-reachable without the requirement of a core point.
red_flags: Defining density-reachability without mentioning core points.
what_tutor_should_explain: The relationship between core points and border points in the context of reachability.
The role of the epsilon parameter in determining if a point is within range of a core point.

evidence_spans.claim: A border point is not a core point but is located within epsilon of at least one core point.

title: Directly Density-Reachable
reviewer_facing_definition:
In DBSCAN, a point q is directly density-reachable from a point p if q lies within the ε-neighborhood of p and p is a core point.

Formally, q is directly density-reachable from p if

q ∈ Nε(p)

and

|Nε(p)| ≥ MinPts.

Direct density-reachability is the basic relation used to define density-reachability: q is density-reachable from p if there exists a chain of points from p to q in which each successive point is directly density-reachable from the preceding point.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What does it mean for a point to be directly density-reachable?
Is point q directly density-reachable from p?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with 'Density-Reachable', which involves a chain of direct reachability.
Contrast with 'Density-Connected', which requires a common point o from which both p and q are reachable.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Asking the student to identify a chain of points to illustrate the difference between direct and general reachability.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing direct density-reachability with general density-reachability.
red_flags: Defining density-reachability without mentioning the requirement for a chain of directly density-reachable points.
what_tutor_should_explain: The distinction between a single direct step and a chain of steps (density-reachability).
How direct density-reachability acts as the atomic unit for clustering connectivity.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor clarifies that direct density-reachability is directional: q may be directly density-reachable from p when p is core, without p necessarily being directly density-reachable from q.

evidence_spans.claim: A point q is density-reachable from p if there is a chain of points where each subsequent point is directly density-reachable from the previous one.

title: Entropy (Node)
reviewer_facing_definition:
In a decision tree, the entropy of a node is an impurity measure that represents how mixed or uncertain the class labels are among the instances in that node.

For a node or dataset D with C classes,

Entropy(D) = -Σ_i p_i log2(p_i),

where p_i is the proportion of instances in class i.

A pure node, containing instances from only one class, has entropy 0. In a binary classification problem, entropy is maximal at 1 when the two classes occur in equal proportions. Decision-tree splits can be evaluated by comparing the entropy of the parent node with the weighted entropy of the resulting child nodes.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: How do we measure the entropy when splitting a node?
What is split information in decision trees?
Does the split result in equally-sized child nodes?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Information Gain or Gini Index, which measure impurity/gain rather than the intrinsic information of the split itself.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Asking the student to evaluate if a split creates many small nodes versus a few large nodes.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing the entropy of the split (split information) with the entropy of the class distribution within a node.
red_flags: Defining entropy only as a measure of class purity without mentioning the split information aspect of node partitioning.
what_tutor_should_explain: The relationship between split information and the distribution of child node sizes.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor distinguishes node entropy from Split Information, explaining that node entropy measures class-label impurity within a node, whereas Split Information measures how the instances are distributed among the child nodes created by a split.

evidence_spans.claim: Split information measures the entropy of splitting a node into its child nodes.
Split information evaluates if a node split results in a larger number of equally-sized child nodes.

title: Euclidean Distance
reviewer_facing_definition: Euclidean distance is defined as the straight-line distance between two points. In practical data mining applications, such as calculating the similarity or dissimilarity between individuals, this measure can be sensitive to the scale of the data; for instance, attributes with larger numerical ranges, such as income values, may dominate the overall calculation.

Why does income dominate the Euclidean distance calculation?

acceptable_teaching_moves: Using a geometric analogy of a straight line to explain the distance.
Providing an example of how a high-value attribute dominates the sum of squares.
common_confusions_or_errors: Ignoring the impact of different attribute scales on the distance calculation.
red_flags: Confusing Euclidean distance with Manhattan distance (grid-based distance).
what_tutor_should_explain: The concept of straight-line distance between two points.
How attributes with larger scales (e.g., income) can disproportionately influence the distance result.

In calculations of similarity or dissimilarity, such as with Euclidean distance, attributes like income values can dominate the calculation.

title: Exhaustive Search
reviewer_facing_definition: Exhaustive search is a method used to guarantee optimality by visiting all possible states. While it is the only approach that provides such a guarantee, it is possible to find an optimal subset without visiting every state by employing exact algorithms, such as branch and bound or backtracking.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: Does exhaustive search always find the best subset?
What happens if we visit every possible state?
Can we get the optimal result without an exhaustive search?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Heuristic Search or Random Generation, which do not guarantee optimality.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Asking the student if there are ways to find the optimal subset without checking every single combination.
common_confusions_or_errors: Assuming that only exhaustive search can find an optimal subset, overlooking other exact algorithms.
red_flags: Claiming that backtracking is a form of exhaustive search that visits all states.
what_tutor_should_explain: The relationship between visiting all states and the guarantee of optimality.
How exact algorithms like backtracking and branch and bound can find optimal subsets more efficiently than a naive exhaustive search.

evidence_spans.claim: Exhaustive search is the only method that can guarantee optimality.
Optimal subsets can be found without visiting all possible states using exact algorithms like branch and bound and backtracking.

title: External Index: Entropy
reviewer_facing_definition:
Entropy is a supervised or external cluster-validity measure that evaluates how well the discovered clusters correspond to known class labels by measuring the extent to which each cluster contains objects from a single class.

For cluster i, let

pij = mij / mi,

where mij is the number of objects of class j in cluster i and mi is the total number of objects in cluster i.

The entropy of cluster i is

ei = -Σj pij log2(pij).

The overall entropy of a clustering is obtained by taking a weighted average of the cluster entropies according to cluster size.

Lower entropy indicates greater class purity, and an entropy of 0 indicates that a cluster contains objects from only one class.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What does an entropy of 1 mean for a split?
How is the external index used to evaluate clusters?
When is weighted entropy equal to zero?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Gini index, which is also mentioned as being equal to zero for children in similar contexts.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Comparing entropy to the Gini index.
Explaining the p-value calculation for external indices.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing high entropy (disorder) with high clustering quality.
red_flags: Claiming that a high entropy value for a split indicates a high-quality cluster.
what_tutor_should_explain: The significance of entropy values (0 vs 1) in the context of data splits.
The general goal of maximizing external index values for better clustering.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor distinguishes entropy used as an external clustering index from entropy used in decision-tree splitting, and does not interpret lower or higher clustering entropy using the decision-tree split context.

evidence_spans.claim: Weighted entropy is equal to zero for children in certain clustering/splitting contexts.
The entropy of a split involving a specific variable can be close to 1.
For external indices, larger values are generally more desirable.
The p-value of an external index can be defined as the fraction of cases where the index exceeds a baseline value m0.

title: External Index: F-Measure
reviewer_facing_definition:
The F-measure is an external cluster-validity measure that combines precision and recall to evaluate a cluster with respect to a specified class.

For cluster i and class j,

F(i, j) =
2 × precision(i, j) × recall(i, j)
divided by
precision(i, j) + recall(i, j).

Precision measures the fraction of the cluster that belongs to the specified class, while recall measures the fraction of all objects of that class that are contained in the cluster.

Thus, the F-measure is high when a cluster both contains mainly objects from the specified class and captures most of the objects belonging to that class.

matching_cues: compare the clustering against the true classes
likely_dialogue_surface_forms: How do I use the F-Measure for clustering?
What is the external index F-Measure?
Can we use information not in the data set to evaluate clusters?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with internal indices (e.g., SSE, Silhouette Coefficient) which do not use external class labels.
Distinguish from other external indices like Purity, Precision, or Recall.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Asking the student to identify where the 'external' information comes from in a real-world scenario.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing external indices with internal indices that only use the data's intrinsic properties.
red_flags: Claiming that F-Measure can be calculated without any external labels or ground truth.
what_tutor_should_explain: The definition of an external index as a supervised measure.
The fact that external indices rely on information (like ground truth labels) not found in the dataset.

evidence_spans.claim: Supervised measures, known as external indices, utilize information that is not contained within the data set.

title: External Index: Precision
reviewer_facing_definition:
Precision is an external cluster-validity measure that evaluates a cluster with respect to a specified class.

For cluster i and class j,

precision(i, j) = mij / mi,

where mij is the number of objects in cluster i that belong to class j, and mi is the total number of objects in cluster i.

Thus, precision measures the fraction of a cluster that consists of objects from the specified class. A higher precision indicates that a larger proportion of the cluster belongs to that class.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: How do we calculate the external index for precision?
What is the precision external index?
Comparing original labels to randomized labels using an external index
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with other external indices such as Purity, Recall, F-Measure, or Rand Index.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Explain the process of computing the index for both original and randomized label sets to establish a baseline.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing external indices (which require ground truth labels) with internal indices (which do not).
red_flags: Applying the external index without having a set of original/ground-truth labels.
what_tutor_should_explain: The role of the external index in comparing original clustering labels against randomized labels.

evidence_spans.claim: The external index can be computed for both an original set of labels and randomized sets of labels.

title: External Index: Recall
reviewer_facing_definition:
Recall is an external cluster-validity measure that evaluates a cluster with respect to a specified class.

For cluster i and class j,

recall(i, j) = mij / mj,

where mij is the number of objects of class j contained in cluster i, and mj is the total number of objects belonging to class j.

title: Filter vs. Wrapper Trade-off
reviewer_facing_definition:
The filter-versus-wrapper trade-off in feature selection concerns how feature subsets are evaluated.

Filter methods evaluate features using criteria that are independent of the learning algorithm. They are generally faster, computationally cheaper, can handle larger data sets, and produce feature subsets that can be used with different learning algorithms.

Wrapper methods use the target learning algorithm itself to evaluate candidate feature subsets according to predictive performance. This allows them to exploit the characteristics of a particular learner and potentially obtain better feature subsets for that learner, but they require greater computational cost and can be more susceptible to overfitting.

Thus, the trade-off is mainly between the speed and generality of filters and the learner-specific predictive optimization of wrappers.

title: Gini Index
reviewer_facing_definition:
The Gini Index is an impurity measure used in decision tree learning to measure how mixed the class labels are within a node.

For a node t,

Gini(t) = 1 - Σ_i p_i(t)^2,

where p_i(t) is the proportion of instances at node t belonging to class i. A pure node has a Gini Index of 0, while more mixed class distributions have higher Gini values.

To evaluate an attribute test condition, the Gini indices of the resulting child nodes are combined as a weighted average according to the number of instances in each child. The preferred split is the one that produces the lowest weighted child-node Gini, equivalently the greatest reduction in impurity.

title: Handling Missing Values in NB
reviewer_facing_definition:
Naive Bayes can handle missing attribute values without necessarily imputing them.

During training, missing values for an attribute are ignored when estimating the conditional probability for that attribute.

During classification, if some attribute values of a test instance are missing, the posterior probability is computed using only the observed, non-missing attributes.

However, this approach may produce inaccurate posterior estimates if the occurrence of missing values depends on the class label.

title: ID3 Algorithm
reviewer_facing_definition:
The ID3 algorithm is a decision tree classification algorithm that follows a greedy, top-down, recursive approach to constructing a decision tree.

Starting from the training instances at the root, a node containing instances from more than one class is split using an attribute test condition. ID3 uses entropy as its impurity measure, so the reduction in entropy produced by a split is measured by Information Gain. A better split produces a larger reduction in entropy.

After a split, the training instances are distributed among the resulting child nodes and the procedure is recursively applied to the children. Nodes that no longer require further splitting become leaf nodes and are assigned class labels.

title: Split Information
reviewer_facing_definition:
Split Information measures how an attribute divides the instances of a parent node among the child nodes produced by a split.

If attribute A divides dataset D into p child subsets D1, D2, ..., Dp, then:

SplitInfo(A) = -Σ_j (|Dj| / |D|) log2(|Dj| / |D|).

Split Information becomes larger when an attribute creates many child nodes, especially when those child nodes are similarly sized. It is used as the denominator of Gain Ratio to reduce Information Gain's preference for attributes that create many branches.

title: K-Means Complexity
reviewer_facing_definition:
For K-means, the time complexity is

O(I × K × m × n),

where I is the number of iterations required for convergence, K is the number of clusters, m is the number of data points, and n is the number of attributes.

Since the number of iterations I is often small and can usually be bounded, and K is typically much smaller than m, K-means is often regarded as approximately linear in the number of data points m.

Its space complexity is

O((m + K)n),

because the algorithm mainly stores the m data points and K centroids.

title: Misclassification Rate
reviewer_facing_definition:
The misclassification rate, also called classification error, is an impurity measure for a decision-tree node. It measures the fraction of instances that would be misclassified if the node were assigned to its majority class.

For a node t,

Classification error(t) = 1 - max_i p_i(t),

where p_i(t) is the proportion of instances at node t that belong to class i.

When evaluating an attribute test condition, the misclassification rates of the resulting child nodes are combined using a weighted average. A split is preferred when it reduces impurity, meaning that the weighted impurity of the child nodes is lower than that of the parent node.

title: NB Classification Phase
reviewer_facing_definition:
The Naive Bayes classification phase is the stage in which the learned model is applied to a new or unseen instance to predict its class label.

For each possible class y, Naive Bayes combines the learned prior probability P(y) with the class-conditional probabilities of the observed attribute values:

P(y | x) ∝ P(y) ∏i P(xi | y).

A score is computed for each candidate class, and the instance is assigned to the class with the largest posterior score. This application of the learned model to an unseen instance corresponds to the deduction phase of classification.

title: NB Learning Phase

The learned prior and class-conditional probabilities are then used during prediction to compute class scores or posterior probabilities for new instances.

title: Properties of a Similarity Function
reviewer_facing_definition:
A similarity function measures the degree to which two objects are alike, with larger values indicating greater similarity.

A similarity function typically satisfies symmetry:

s(x, y) = s(y, x).

Unlike a metric distance function, a similarity function generally does not have an equivalent requirement corresponding to the triangle inequality.

title: Sequential Backward Generation (SBG)
reviewer_facing_definition:
Sequential Backward Generation (SBG) is a feature-subset generation method that starts with the full set of features.

At each step, it identifies the least relevant or worst feature and removes it from the current feature set F.

The process continues until the stopping criterion is reached, such as when the removed-feature set S no longer satisfies U or when F becomes empty.

When removing the last feature causes the criterion to fail, that feature is added back so that the previous acceptable feature subset is returned.

SBG is a heuristic backward-search method because it removes features sequentially rather than evaluating every possible feature subset.

title: Significance Level (alpha)
reviewer_facing_definition:
The significance level, α, is a predefined threshold used in statistical hypothesis testing to determine when a result is considered statistically significant.

It represents the probability of making a Type I error, that is, falsely rejecting the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is true.

A result is considered statistically significant when its p-value is less than α. Common choices for α are 0.05 and 0.01.

Choosing α also affects the balance between Type I and Type II errors: increasing the critical region can increase power and reduce Type II errors, but it also increases the risk of Type I errors.

title: Significance Level and p-value
reviewer_facing_definition:
The p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of obtaining the observed test statistic or something more extreme.

The significance level, α, is a predefined threshold used to decide whether a p-value is statistically significant. For a single test, the null hypothesis is rejected when the p-value is below α.

In the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure for multiple hypothesis testing, the m p-values are first ordered from smallest to largest:

p1 ≤ p2 ≤ ... ≤ pm.

A different threshold is assigned to each ordered p-value:

αi = iα / m.

Thus, the threshold for the smallest p-value is α/m, the same as the Bonferroni threshold, while the threshold for the largest p-value is α.

The procedure finds the largest index k for which

pk ≤ kα/m,

and declares the first k ordered p-values significant.

In this way, BH provides a less conservative alternative to Bonferroni by controlling the False Discovery Rate while generally providing greater statistical power.

title: Centroid Initialization Sensitivity
reviewer_facing_definition:
Centroid initialization sensitivity refers to the dependence of the final K-Means clustering on the initial positions chosen for the centroids.

Because K-Means converges only to a local minimum of its objective function, different initial centroid choices can lead to different cluster assignments and different total SSE values. Some starting configurations may lead to a good or globally optimal clustering, while others may lead to a suboptimal local minimum.

A common way to reduce this problem is to run K-Means several times with different initial centroids and select the clustering with the lowest SSE. Other initialization methods can also be used to obtain better starting centroids.

title: Divisive (Top-Down) Clustering
reviewer_facing_definition:
Divisive hierarchical clustering is a top-down clustering approach that begins with all data objects in one cluster and repeatedly splits clusters into smaller clusters.

At each stage, a divisive method must determine which cluster should be split, how that cluster should be divided, and when the splitting process should stop. Splitting can continue until every object forms a singleton cluster or until another stopping criterion is reached.

Different divisive algorithms use different splitting rules. Examples include Bisecting K-Means, which splits a selected cluster using K-Means with K = 2, and MST-based divisive clustering.

In the MST divisive hierarchical algorithm, a minimum spanning tree is first constructed from the dissimilarity graph. The hierarchy is then produced by repeatedly removing the edge with the largest dissimilarity, thereby separating the data into increasingly smaller clusters.

title: Information Gain (Feature Goodness)
reviewer_facing_definition:
Information Gain is a feature-goodness measure that evaluates how much a feature reduces uncertainty about the class.

Given a dataset D that is divided by feature A into subsets D1, D2, ..., Dp, Information Gain is

IG(A) = I(D) - Σj (|Dj| / |D|) I(Dj),

where I(D) is the class uncertainty before using the feature and the second term is the expected uncertainty after splitting on the feature.

A feature with higher Information Gain is preferred because it produces a greater reduction in class uncertainty.

Information Gain has a tendency to favor features with many distinct values, so Information Gain Ratio can be used to reduce this bias.

FOIL's Information Gain is a related but different measure used in rule-growing algorithms such as RIPPER. It evaluates candidate conjuncts using both improvement in rule accuracy and the number of positive examples covered:

FOILGain = p1 × [log2(p1/(p1+n1)) - log2(p0/(p0+n0))].

title: One-sided vs. Two-sided Tests
reviewer_facing_definition:
A one-sided test considers extreme values of the test statistic in only one direction.

A right-tailed test treats unusually large values as evidence against the null hypothesis, while a left-tailed test treats unusually small values as evidence against the null hypothesis. The p-value is therefore calculated from the corresponding single tail of the null distribution.

A two-sided test considers extreme values in both directions. Its p-value includes probabilities from both tails of the null distribution.

For a significance level α, a one-sided test places the critical probability α in one tail, whereas a two-sided test divides the critical probability between the two tails. For example, when α = 0.05, a symmetric two-sided test has 0.025 in each tail, while a one-sided test has the full 0.05 in one tail.

The appropriate choice depends on whether the hypothesis is directional or whether departures from the null hypothesis in either direction are of interest.

reviewer_facing_definition:
Accuracy is a traditional measure of classification performance that represents the fraction of instances whose class labels are predicted correctly.

For an entire classifier:

Accuracy = number of correct predictions / total number of predictions.

In the specific context of a classification rule, rule accuracy, also called the confidence factor, is the fraction of instances triggered by the rule whose class labels equal the rule's target class.

Accuracy can be misleading when the test data has class imbalance because a classifier can achieve high accuracy by predicting the majority class while performing poorly on the minority class.

title: Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC)
reviewer_facing_definition: The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is a performance metric for machine learning algorithms used to summarize the aggregate behavior of a classifier across all operating points. A perfect classifier achieves an AUC of 1, while an algorithm performing random guessing results in an AUC of 0.5. While useful for aggregate performance summary, AUC has limitations when comparing classifiers; a higher AUC for one algorithm does not necessarily mean it is always better than another unless its ROC curve strictly dominates the other across all operating points. If ROC curves intersect, assessing relative quality via AUC becomes difficult.
sibling_kc_names: Threshold Effect on Precision, Recall, F1

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What does the AUC value mean?
Is a higher AUC always better?
How do I interpret the area under the ROC curve?
Comparing two models using AUC
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with the ROC Curve itself, which shows performance at specific operating points rather than an aggregate summary.
Contrast with Precision-Recall (PR) curves, which are noted as an alternative for aggregate performance, particularly with class imbalance.
do_not_confuse_with: ROC Curve (the plot vs the area metric)

acceptable_teaching_moves: Using a visual example of intersecting ROC curves to demonstrate why AUC can be misleading.
Comparing the AUC of a random classifier (0.5) to a perfect one (1.0) to establish a scale.
common_confusions_or_errors: Assuming that Algorithm A is strictly better than Algorithm B simply because AUC(A) > AUC(B).
Confusing the aggregate AUC metric with the point-by-point ROC curve.
red_flags: Claiming AUC is the definitive way to determine the 'better' algorithm without mentioning dominance or intersection.
what_tutor_should_explain: The meaning of AUC values 0.5 and 1.0.
The concept of dominance in ROC curves and why a higher AUC doesn't automatically imply a superior model.
The limitation of AUC when ROC curves intersect.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor treats AUC as equivalent to classification accuracy at a particular decision threshold, rather than as a measure of ranking performance across score thresholds.

evidence_spans.claim: AUC is a performance metric for machine learning algorithms that summarizes aggregate behavior across all operating points.
A perfect classifier has an AUC of 1, while random guessing results in an AUC of 0.5.
A higher AUC does not necessarily mean one algorithm is always better than another unless its ROC curve dominates the other across all operating points.
If ROC curves of two classifiers intersect, it is difficult to assess relative quality using the AUC measure.

title: Bisecting K-Means
reviewer_facing_definition: Bisecting K-Means is a clustering approach that begins with a single cluster containing all data points. The process involves repeatedly selecting one cluster and splitting it into two separate clusters by applying the basic K-Means algorithm with K = 2. This iterative bisection continues until the target number of clusters is achieved.

Does it start with one cluster containing all points?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with standard K-Means Algorithm, which typically initializes K centroids simultaneously rather than iteratively splitting a single global cluster.

Prompting the student to explain how the algorithm decides when to stop splitting.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing the global K (final number of clusters) with the local K=2 used for the bisection step.
red_flags: Claiming that Bisecting K-Means initializes all K centroids at once.

The use of K=2 for each individual split.
The iterative nature of the process until the desired cluster count is reached.

evidence_spans.claim: Bisecting K-Means starts with one cluster containing all points.
The algorithm repeatedly splits one selected cluster into two using basic K-Means with K = 2 until the desired number of clusters is reached.

title: Boosting
reviewer_facing_definition: Boosting is an iterative procedure used to adaptively change the distribution of training examples for learning base classifiers, ensuring they increasingly focus on examples that are difficult to classify. Unlike bagging, boosting assigns a weight to each training example and updates these weights at the end of each boosting round; specifically, weights are increased for incorrectly classified examples and decreased for correctly classified ones. While this approach can reduce both bias and variance in final predictions, its tendency to focus on wrongly classified examples can make the technique susceptible to overfitting, potentially leading to poor generalization performance.

What is the difference between bagging and boosting?

Can boosting overfit?

common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing boosting with bagging (both are ensemble methods but differ in how they handle training data).
red_flags: Claiming boosting is immune to overfitting.
Suggesting that all training examples maintain equal weights throughout the process.

How focusing on difficult examples reduces bias and variance.
The trade-off between performance improvement and the risk of overfitting.

Unlike bagging, boosting assigns and adaptively updates weights for training examples at the end of each round.
Weights are increased for incorrectly classified examples and decreased for correctly classified ones to force the classifier to focus on difficult examples.
Boosting can be susceptible to overfitting and poor generalization due to its focus on wrongly classified examples.

title: Border Point
reviewer_facing_definition: A border point is a data point that is not a core point itself, but is located within the neighborhood of at least one core point. Because a border point can fall within the neighborhoods of multiple core points, it is assigned to one of the clusters associated with its neighboring core points. This assignment process can become ambiguous in cases where the border point touches core points belonging to different clusters.

How do you assign a border point to a cluster?
Can a point be a border point for two clusters?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Core Point: Core points meet density requirements; border points do not but are reachable from core points.
Contrast with Noise Point: Noise points are neither core points nor border points.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Asking the student to identify if a point meets the core point criteria before checking if it is a border point.
Using a scenario where a point is equidistant from two different cluster cores to illustrate assignment ambiguity.

Claiming border points are always uniquely assigned to a single cluster without ambiguity.

The mechanism for assigning a border point to a cluster when it is adjacent to multiple core points.

Border points are assigned to one of the clusters of their associated core points.

title: Class Imbalance Problem
reviewer_facing_definition: Class imbalance, also referred to as skew, occurs in datasets where there is a disproportionate number of instances belonging to different classes. This is common in scenarios such as credit card fraud detection, where fraudulent transactions are greatly outnumbered by legitimate ones, or healthcare applications involving rare diseases. This imbalance impacts classifiers if the minority class is not well-represented in the training set. Furthermore, traditional accuracy is not a well-suited metric for evaluating models in the presence of class imbalance in test data, as a trivial model can achieve high accuracy by simply predicting the majority class while failing to detect minority class activities. To address this, undersampling and oversampling can be used to generate balanced training sets.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What happens when one class is much larger than the other?
Why is accuracy bad for imbalanced data?
How do I handle skew in my dataset?
sibling_contrast_notes: Distinguish from specific mitigation techniques like SMOTE (Oversampling) or Undersampling, which are solutions to this problem.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Using the credit card fraud example to illustrate how a trivial model can have 99% accuracy but zero utility.
Comparing the representation of minority vs. majority classes in training data.
common_confusions_or_errors: Assuming high accuracy indicates a successful model in an imbalanced dataset.
Confusing the problem (imbalance) with the solution (oversampling/undersampling).
red_flags: Suggesting accuracy as the primary metric for a skewed dataset.
what_tutor_should_explain: The definition of class imbalance/skew.
Why accuracy is misleading when classes are disproportionate.
The general goal of creating balanced training sets via sampling.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor claims that balancing an imbalanced training set through undersampling or oversampling necessarily improves the resulting classifier without introducing any disadvantages.

evidence_spans.claim: Class imbalance, or skew, is the property of datasets having a disproportionate number of instances belonging to different classes.
Examples of class imbalance include rare disease diagnosis in healthcare and fraudulent transactions in credit card data.
Classifiers are impacted if the minority class is not well-represented in the training set.

title: Cluster Definition
reviewer_facing_definition:
A cluster is a group of data objects regarded as belonging together according to a particular notion of similarity, proximity, connectivity, density, or shared properties. Different clustering approaches therefore use different definitions of what constitutes a cluster.

In a graph-based definition, where nodes represent objects and links represent connections, a cluster can be defined as a connected component: a group of objects connected to one another with no connections to objects outside the group.

A specific graph-based form is a contiguity-based cluster, where two objects are connected only if they are within a specified distance. Consequently, each object in the cluster is closer to some other object in the same cluster than to any point in another cluster. This definition can capture irregular or intertwined clusters, but it is sensitive to noise because a small bridge of points can connect and merge two otherwise distinct clusters.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What is a cluster in a graph?
How do contiguity-based clusters work?
What happens when noise affects cluster merging?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with distance-based metrics like Inter-cluster or Intra-cluster distance by focusing on connectivity rather than just distance values.
do_not_confuse_with: General distance metrics without connectivity requirements

acceptable_teaching_moves: Using a graph analogy (nodes and links) to explain connected components.
Comparing irregular clusters to spherical clusters to show the utility of the graph-based definition.
common_confusions_or_errors: Assuming all clusters are spherical or simple shapes.
Overlooking the fact that a single bridge of points can merge two separate clusters in graph-based definitions.
red_flags: Defining clusters solely by distance without mentioning connectivity or connected components in a graph context.
what_tutor_should_explain: The requirement that a cluster has no connections to objects outside the group.
The specific distance constraint in contiguity-based clustering.
How 'noise' or a 'bridge of points' can lead to the merging of distinct clusters.

evidence_spans.claim: In graph-represented data, a cluster is a connected component consisting of objects connected to each other but not to objects outside the group.
Contiguity-based clusters are graph-based clusters where objects are connected only if they are within a specified distance of each other.
Graph-based definitions are useful for irregular or intertwined clusters but can be compromised by noise, where a small bridge of points merges distinct clusters.

title: Cohesion
reviewer_facing_definition: Cohesion is a measure of cluster quality that can be quantified as the sum of the pairwise similarities of all objects within a cluster. In terms of calculation, it is expressed as the sum of the proximity of each object to the cluster center. In the context of cluster evaluation, minimizing the sum of squared errors (SSE), which represents cohesion, is mathematically equivalent to maximizing the sum of squares between clusters (SSB), which represents separation.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What is cohesion in clustering?
How do we calculate the cohesion of a cluster?
Is minimizing SSE the same as maximizing separation?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Separation (SSB), which focuses on the distance between different clusters rather than the internal tightness of a single cluster.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Linking the concept of cohesion to the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE).
Explaining the trade-off or equivalence between cohesion and separation.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing cohesion (internal cluster similarity) with separation (inter-cluster distance).
red_flags: Claiming that increasing SSE improves cohesion.
what_tutor_should_explain: The inverse relationship between minimizing cohesion (SSE) and maximizing separation (SSB).
How proximity to the cluster center defines the internal tightness of the cluster.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor assumes that a numerically larger cohesion value is always better, without distinguishing whether cohesion is being measured using similarity or dissimilarity.

evidence_spans.claim: Minimizing the sum of squared errors (SSE), which represents cohesion, is equivalent to maximizing the sum of squares between clusters (SSB), which represents separation.
Cohesion for a cluster is calculated as the sum of the proximity of objects within that cluster to the cluster center.

title: Confidence Interval for Accuracy
reviewer_facing_definition: A confidence interval for accuracy is used to quantify the inherent uncertainty in a model's performance by providing an interval of parameter values in which an estimated parameter value is guaranteed to fall a certain percentage of times. This percentage is known as the confidence level. To estimate the true performance of a classifier trained over all possible instances, statistical resampling approaches—such as bootstrap sampling (random selection with replacement) or k-fold cross-validation (systematic splitting into subsets)—are used to compute distributions of classification performance measures like accuracy, precision, and recall. These distributions then allow for the production of confidence intervals, such as an interval containing 95% of the distribution for a classifier's accuracy.
sibling_kc_names: Comparing Two Models on Independent Test Sets

sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with point estimates, which provide a single value rather than an interval of uncertainty.
do_not_confuse_with: Simple k-fold cross-validation without the distribution/interval step

acceptable_teaching_moves: Asking the student to explain why a range of values is more informative than a single accuracy score.
Guiding the student to connect bootstrap sampling to the creation of a performance distribution.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing the confidence level with the accuracy percentage itself.
Assuming a single test set result is sufficient to determine a confidence interval without resampling.
red_flags: Student claims a confidence interval can be calculated without a distribution of measures.
Student confuses k-fold cross-validation as a final result rather than a means to estimate the distribution.
what_tutor_should_explain: The difference between a point estimate and a confidence interval.
How resampling (bootstrap/k-fold) creates the distribution necessary to define the interval.
The meaning of the confidence level (e.g., 95%) in the context of the true performance parameter.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor correctly explains that, under the normal-approximation confidence interval for accuracy, increasing the test-set size reduces sampling uncertainty and therefore produces a narrower confidence interval, all else being equal.

Resampling methods like the bootstrap can also estimate the distribution of the support of a frequent itemset.

title: Confusion Matrix
reviewer_facing_definition: A confusion matrix is a table used to evaluate the performance of a classifier by comparing predicted labels against the true labels of instances. In this table, each entry represents the number of instances from a specific class that were predicted to belong to another class. For example, in a binary classification problem, it tracks correct predictions and incorrect predictions, such as instances of class 0 incorrectly predicted as class 1. Beyond basic evaluation, a confusion matrix can be used to define a similarity measure between two classes based on the frequency of misclassifications, though this measure is inherently non-symmetric.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What is a confusion matrix?
How do I turn predictions into a confusion matrix?
How do we use a confusion matrix to see if the model is performing well?
sibling_contrast_notes: The confusion matrix is the raw table of counts from which other metrics like Accuracy, Precision, and Recall are derived.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Using a binary classification example to illustrate correct vs incorrect predictions.
Walking through the process of turning a set of predictions into the matrix before calculating metrics.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing the axis of true labels versus predicted labels.
Assuming the similarity measure derived from the matrix is symmetric.
red_flags: Calculating metrics without first establishing the confusion matrix counts.
Claiming that the number of times x is misclassified as y is the same as y being misclassified as x.
what_tutor_should_explain: The relationship between true labels and predicted labels in the matrix.
How to interpret specific entries (e.g., class i predicted as class j).
The fact that the matrix serves as the foundation for calculating further evaluation metrics.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor claims that a confusion matrix is incorrect simply because predicted classes are placed in rows and actual classes in columns; either orientation can be used if it is labeled clearly and interpreted consistently.

evidence_spans.claim: A confusion matrix is a table that summarizes the performance of a classifier by comparing predicted labels against true labels.
Each entry in the matrix denotes the number of instances from class i predicted to be of class j.
Predictions are first turned into a confusion matrix before calculating further metrics.
A similarity measure between two characters can be defined as the number of times one is misclassified as the other, but this measure is not symmetric.

title: Core Point
reviewer_facing_definition: A core point is a data point located in the interior of a density-based cluster. Formally, a point is classified as a core point if the number of points within its neighborhood—defined by a distance radius (Eps) and potentially SNN similarity—meets or exceeds a user-specified threshold called MinPts. In the context of cluster formation, core points serve as the foundation that starts and expands dense regions.

Asking the student to calculate if a point is 'core' given specific Eps and MinPts values.

what_tutor_should_explain: The relationship between the parameters Eps and MinPts in determining core status.
The role of core points in initiating the expansion of a cluster.

title: DBSCAN Advantages and Limitations
reviewer_facing_definition: DBSCAN offers several advantages over K-means, particularly when the number of clusters is unknown in advance, the data is noisy, or natural clusters are non-spherical and density-separated. Because it utilizes a density-based definition, it can identify clusters of arbitrary shapes and sizes and is relatively resistant to noise. However, DBSCAN has limitations: it struggles with high-dimensional data where density is harder to define and when clusters exhibit widely varying densities. Additionally, it can be computationally expensive if calculating nearest neighbors requires computing all pairwise proximities, a common occurrence in high-dimensional datasets.

Can DBSCAN handle high-dimensional data?
How does DBSCAN deal with noise?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with 'DBSCAN Parameters' by focusing on the outcomes/performance of the algorithm rather than the configuration of eps and minPts.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Comparing a spherical cluster (K-means) with an arbitrary shape (DBSCAN).
Asking the student to identify a scenario where varying densities would hinder DBSCAN.
common_confusions_or_errors: Assuming DBSCAN is always superior to K-means regardless of data density variance.
Overlooking the computational overhead in high-dimensional spaces.
red_flags: Claiming DBSCAN is efficient for all high-dimensional datasets.
Stating that DBSCAN requires the number of clusters to be specified beforehand.
what_tutor_should_explain: The relationship between high-dimensional data and the difficulty of defining density.
Why non-spherical clusters are a challenge for K-means but not for DBSCAN.
The computational cost associated with pairwise proximity calculations.

title: DBSCAN Cluster Definition
reviewer_facing_definition: DBSCAN is a partitional clustering algorithm that assigns each object to a single cluster, though unlike K-means, it discards objects classified as noise. It functions by building clusters around core objects, which allows the algorithm to identify clusters of varying shapes and sizes and remain resilient against outliers. However, DBSCAN's performance is limited when clusters exhibit widely differing densities; for a fixed MinPts, the choice of the Eps threshold can lead to either merging dense clusters and their surrounding noise into one or marking lower-density clusters as noise.

red_flags: Claiming DBSCAN is immune to all density-related issues.
Stating that DBSCAN assigns every single data point to a cluster.
what_tutor_should_explain: The distinction between partitional clustering that includes all points (K-means) versus those that discard noise (DBSCAN).

red_flags: Confusing Eps with a fixed number of neighbors rather than a distance radius.

reviewer_facing_definition: Data cleaning is a preprocessing step used to filter or correct wrong data, such as uncontrolled noise or missing values. This process is essential because without it, data mining algorithms may be unable to handle the data, or the knowledge extracted from the data will lack accuracy. While cleaning involves eliminating inconsistencies and redundant attributes, these actions alone may still result in a large dataset that can slow down the data mining process.

title: Data Integration
reviewer_facing_definition: Data integration is the process of integrating data from different databases to merge examples from various sources into a single data set. This process is complicated by challenges such as uneven examples resulting from different table schemes or attribute names, and inconsistencies where the same concept is represented by different attribute values. Additionally, data integration requires detecting and eliminating redundant attributes that occur when some attributes are calculated from others, which would otherwise increase data set size without scaling the actual information contained.

Redundant attributes, often resulting from attributes calculated from others, must be detected and eliminated to prevent unnecessary increase in data set size.

title: Dendrogram
reviewer_facing_definition: A dendrogram is a tree-like diagram used to graphically display hierarchical clustering. It illustrates the relationships between clusters and subclusters, as well as the sequence in which clusters were either merged (in an agglomerative view) or split (in a divisive view). Beyond visualization, the dendrogram serves a functional role in cluster extraction; specifically, a desired number of clusters (K) can be generated by taking the clusters at a particular level of the dendrogram.

likely_dialogue_surface_forms: What is a dendrogram?
How do I read the tree diagram for clustering?
How many clusters can I get from the dendrogram?
Where do I cut the dendrogram to get K clusters?
sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with nested cluster diagrams, which are also used for two-dimensional points.
Distinguish from the specific algorithms (Agglomerative vs Divisive) that produce the dendrogram.
do_not_confuse_with: K-means clustering (which does not produce a dendrogram)

acceptable_teaching_moves: Asking the student to identify the order of merges from a provided image.
Guiding the student to 'cut' the tree at a certain level to determine the number of clusters.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing the dendrogram with a standard decision tree.
Not understanding that the 'level' of the dendrogram determines the number of clusters extracted.
red_flags: Student believes the dendrogram is only for visualization and cannot be used to determine the number of clusters.
what_tutor_should_explain: The relationship between the height/level of the dendrogram and the number of resulting clusters.
The difference between the agglomerative (merging) and divisive (splitting) perspectives shown in the diagram.

reviewer_criteria.criterion_text: The tutor correctly explains that two dendrograms can represent the same hierarchical clustering even if branches are flipped left-to-right, provided that their nesting and merge structure are the same.

evidence_spans.claim: A dendrogram is a tree-like diagram that graphically displays hierarchical clustering, showing cluster-subcluster relationships and the order of merges (agglomerative) or splits (divisive).
